source.title: From Sharpness to Better Generalization for Speech Deepfake Detection
source.authors: Wen Huang; Xue-Chen Liu; Xin Wang; Junichi Yamagishi; Yanmin Qian

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; no truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies sharpness measurement and sharpness-aware training to speech deepfake detection across unseen datasets and reports results in that new setting. Its out-of-distribution speech results do not test the listed in-distribution versions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Adam-versus-SAM EER results in Table 1, sharpness correlations in Table 2, and qualitative mismatch trends in Figure 1. These concern out-of-distribution speech deepfake detection; none measures the behaviors or exact measures named in V1–V8. Figures 1 and 2 are not extracted as rows because their results are figure-only and the paper's prose does not give specific values for each plotted condition.
record.test_reason: The study uses the sharpness–generalization rationale to motivate SAM, but tests none of V1–V8. Its unscaled, fixed-radius m-sharpness is measured on evaluation data and correlated with evaluation EER, rather than magnitude-aware training sharpness with train–test gaps as V7 specifies. Both training conditions use Adam, so their comparison does not test V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors: they conclude that sharpness reflects domain mismatch, is positively associated with EER in most out-of-domain settings, and that SAM generally improves robustness and stability. These are claims about evaluation-set m-sharpness and detection performance, not V7's magnitude-aware training sharpness and generalization gaps. The results include exceptions to improved EER and stability.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses speech deepfake detection, out-of-distribution datasets, and m-sharpness with SAM; the mapped versions concern image or language settings and other interventions or measures. It uses Adam as the baseline optimizer.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary by model and dataset: some SAM runs have higher EER than Adam, including W2V-Base+Linear on WF and W2V-Large+Linear on FOR; correlation strength also varies by dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM added to Adam usually lowers speech deepfake detection EER, with model- and dataset-dependent exceptions. For example, W2V-Base+Linear improves on 21LA from 5.82 to 3.39 but worsens on WF from 30.34 to 36.95.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding SAM to Adam can improve speech deepfake detection on unseen conditions, but improvements depend on the model and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 reports positive correlations between evaluation-set m-sharpness and EER across systems: PCC is 0.89 on ITW, 0.65 on 21LA and ADD, and 0.13 on 19LA. This is neither magnitude-aware sharpness nor a train–test-gap measurement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fixed-radius evaluation-set m-sharpness correlates positively with speech deepfake detection EER, with strength varying across datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 2 reports increased sharpness for unseen Japanese speech, more unseen attacks, and channel variation, but little change with speaker count; channel sensitivity is weaker for W2V-Base+Linear.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Evaluation-set m-sharpness responds to some speech domain mismatches, depending on the mismatch factor and model.

record.problems: The paper studies out-of-distribution speech detection rather than the mapped in-distribution claim. Table 2's correlation coefficients are reported without their p-values in the supplied text, though the authors state that significance is present in five out-of-domain datasets. The table compares EER outcomes across three runs; no training-error values are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 has 98 optimizer-by-model-by-dataset entries. Rows R01–R60 cover the first three model groups, AASIST, W2V-Base+Linear, and W2V-Base+AASIST, plus W2V-Large+Linear on 19LA, 21LA, 21DF, ITW, and FOR. The remaining Table 1 entries are omitted due to the 60-row cap: W2V-Large+Linear on WF, ADD, and SC; all W2V-Large+AASIST, W2V-XLSR+Linear, and W2V-XLSR+AASIST entries. Table 2's individual correlation rows and Figure 1 mismatch sharpness results are also not extracted because the cap is reached and no mapped version directly matches those measures.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization, and chance performance under random labels.
Width beyond interpolation, zero training error, and subsequent test-error trends.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive methods versus SGD or momentum SGD and the effects of tuning, decoupled weight decay, or optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under matched epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.

Magnitude-aware training sharpness versus train–test gaps among a convolutional family at similarly low training loss, including comparison with norm and margin measures. Evaluation-set m-sharpness versus EER does not test this relationship.
Removing examples selected by label memorization versus random removal and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted Table 1 values and baselines match the supplied text. States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8; the EER values themselves are readable. Table 1 contains 112 optimizer-by-model-by-dataset entries, not 98. R59–R60 already cover W2V-Large+Linear on WF, contrary to rows_left_out. Other omitted results are declared and do not bear on a listed version. Table 2 significance formatting is unavailable in the plain text; the prose reports significance in five of six out-of-domain datasets without identifying all five. The text also inconsistently reports 24 correlation systems despite Table 1 listing 14 model/optimizer combinations.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label held-out performance.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum on the listed benchmarks.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus train-test gaps among similarly low-training-loss networks; the paper uses m-sharpness and EER across speech-domain shifts.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.
